title: Web-CogReasoner: Knowledge-Induced Cognitive Reasoning
one_liner: A web agent reasons better when you first teach it structured facts, concepts, and procedures about the websites it will navigate.
lead: Today's web agents can see and click on a webpage, but they often stumble because they do not understand what they are looking at. This paper argues that a web agent needs three kinds of knowledge — raw facts, high-level concepts, and step-by-step procedures — before it can think through a complex web task. The authors built a dataset from real websites and a reasoning system that learns all three kinds of knowledge together, allowing the agent to generalize to brand-new tasks it has never seen.

paras: A modern web agent uses a vision model (a neural network trained to understand pictures) to look at a webpage and decide what button to click next. This works for simple tasks — click the login link, fill in a form — but falls apart on harder ones. The agent sees labels and buttons, but does not grasp what they mean. When it sees a button labeled 'Billing', it has only learned from pixels what that button looks like; it does not understand that 'Billing' is about payment management, whereas 'Settings' is about account configuration. Because the agent is pattern-matching on visual appearance alone, it cannot reason about consequences of clicking.

A beginner would think: just show the model more examples of web tasks and it will learn. But that fails because each website is different. A model trained on 100 examples from a booking site will not automatically know what to do on a bank site or an e-commerce site. The model has memorized patterns, not principles. For example, the visual appearance of a button labeled 'Billing' looks completely different from one labeled 'Settings' on different websites; if the model learned only from pixel patterns, it has no way to know that both are configuration actions, so when it sees a new 'Billing' button in a layout it has never seen, it cannot reuse what it learned before.

callout.html: Before teaching the agent to act, teach it three types of knowledge: which facts are true (product names, prices), which high-level concepts explain the workflow (checkout means payment), and which procedures work (first add to cart, then checkout).

steps.text: Extract facts, concepts, procedures from real websites into a structured dataset.
Train the agent to retrieve and use each knowledge type during reasoning.
Agent explains each action: which concept did it recognize? why that procedure?
Agent faces websites it has never trained on; structured knowledge transfers.
Compare success rate on familiar tasks versus unseen tasks; measure the knowledge gap.

paras: The paper changes what knowledge the agent learns before acting. Instead of learning only patterns in examples, the agent learns three explicit, structured types of knowledge: factual (a shopping cart holds items), conceptual (categories organize behavior), and procedural (steps in a workflow). The agent is trained to explicitly ground its reasoning in this knowledge during decision-making.

hidden.name: structural knowledge coverage across domains
paras: The paper introduces a hidden measure: how much of the three knowledge types does the agent actually use and remember? The paper calls this the agent's 'cognitive grounding' — the fraction of reasoning steps where the agent draws on factual, conceptual, or procedural knowledge instead of guessing. A web agent that memorizes task examples may score low on this measure: it performs the task but for the wrong reasons.

The paper estimates this by building a structured dataset (Web-CogDataset) from 14 real websites. Each dataset entry is tagged by knowledge type: factual (a color name and price), conceptual (this is a filtering step), procedural (after clicking, wait for page load). During training, the agent learns to retrieve and cite the right knowledge for each step. The more it uses real knowledge, the better it generalizes to unseen sites, because structured knowledge is site-agnostic — once the agent understands that a 'checkout' conceptually means confirming and paying, that understanding works on any website with a checkout flow, regardless of visual design.

heat.caption: Darker cells mean the agent grounded that reasoning step in structured knowledge.

reads.html: Before solving a task, the agent reviews facts (prices), concepts (workflow categories), and procedures (click-then-wait patterns) so it understands what it is looking at.

The paper operationalizes knowledge acquisition through a Chain-of-Thought framework where the agent's reasoning steps are explicitly paired with knowledge domain citations; evaluation measures success on both memorized and unseen tasks to isolate the effect of structural knowledge.

mechanism.h2: Why structured knowledge makes reasoning work
paras: When a web agent sees a button, it has no idea what clicking it does. It may have learned from past examples that certain visual patterns predict certain outcomes, but that learning is fragile. Show the agent a different website layout and it fails. Structured knowledge fixes this by giving the agent a shared vocabulary. If the agent knows 'a checkout button always leads to payment entry' (a conceptual fact), it can apply that rule on any website, because the meaning of checkout is stable across sites even if the button looks different — the logic is the same. If it knows 'after filling a password field, check if an error message appears before clicking submit' (a procedure), it applies that on any site, because the workflow of validation-then-submit is universal.

The paper's mechanism has two parts. First, the agent learns three types of knowledge separately: facts are like a lookup table (what is the price of this item?), concepts are like categories (what does this button belong to?), and procedures are like recipes (what is the sequence of actions?). Second, during reasoning, the agent is trained to explicitly cite which knowledge it used for each step. This forces the agent to 'think out loud' — for example, 'I see a button labeled Buy. This matches the concept of a purchase action. The procedure for purchase is: add to cart, then click checkout, then wait.' This reasoning is more likely to work on a new website because the agent is following principles, not memorizing screenshots.

stages.s: Reason step-by-step: cite which knowledge for each choice
Decision and explanation grounded in knowledge

math.words: The reasoning score for a task is the number of successful steps minus a penalty for steps not grounded in structured knowledge.
math.equation: score = sum_steps (1 if cited_knowledge[step] else 0.1) - lambda * (1 - fraction_knowledge_used)
symbols: whether the step explicitly drew from factual, conceptual, or procedural knowledge (1 if yes, 0.1 if guessed)
the ratio of reasoning steps grounded in structured knowledge to total steps (0 to 1)
how much to penalize reasoning that avoids structured knowledge (a weight, e.g. 0.3)

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Task: click the checkout button. Five reasoning steps: identify page (cite Conceptual), find button (cite Factual), wait for page load (cite Procedural), verify order (cite Factual), click submit (cite Procedural).
All 5 steps cite knowledge, so cited_knowledge = [1, 1, 1, 1, 1], sum = 5. Fraction used = 5/5 = 1.0.
Contrast: a memorized-only agent might complete the task but guess on 2 steps. Cited = [1, 0.1, 0.1, 1, 1], sum = 3.2. Fraction = 3/5 = 0.6.

math.note: Steps that draw on knowledge earn full credit; steps without knowledge are penalized, rewarding the agent to build and use structured reasoning.

charts.title: Without structured knowledge
charts.note: Agent trained only on examples memorizes task patterns but fails on new layouts.

charts.title: With structured knowledge
charts.note: Agent trained with factual, conceptual, procedural knowledge transfers principles to unseen sites.

items.html: If the dataset does not cover a fact or procedure the agent needs on a new website, the agent cannot cite it. For example, if the training data never showed a 'two-factor authentication' procedure, the agent will stumble when it encounters one.
Two websites may use the same label differently (a 'Settings' button might mean account settings on one site and payment settings on another). The agent may cite the wrong concept and fail.

items.b: Reasoning becomes brittle if knowledge is vague.
items.html: If the conceptual knowledge says 'a button is a call to action' without detail, the agent has no way to predict the consequences of clicking.

The dataset is curated carefully: facts are specific (product X costs Y dollars), concepts are precise (checkout is distinct from payment entry), procedures are step-by-step. This lets the agent cite knowledge with confidence and transfer to new sites.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a toy dataset: three websites (a shopping site, a booking site, a forum) with 30 tasks total. Manually tag each task with factual, conceptual, and procedural knowledge needed. Train one agent to memorize patterns from examples, and a second agent using the knowledge framework. On the training websites, both should do well. On three held-out new websites (never seen in training), measure the success rate of each agent.
demo.closing: The demo must show that the agent trained with structured knowledge generalizes at least 2x better to new websites than the baseline, because structured knowledge is site-independent — principles like 'checkout means payment' or 'fill then validate' work on unfamiliar layouts, whereas memorized visual patterns do not.
